summary: Defines the structure of the RPKI distributed repository. Each publication point is a directory holding certificates, revocation lists and signed objects. It specifies naming of files, what each publication point contains, and a suggested layout for a local cache that helps with synchronizing.

plainLanguage.summary: RPKI documents need to be stored somewhere organized. This says how each folder is laid out, how files are named, and how a local copy should be kept in sync.

subtitle: How the RPKI stores its certificates, revocation lists and signed objects so routers' validators can find and fetch them.

tldr.problem: To validate RPKI attestations, relying parties need access to every certificate, CRL and signed object in the system, so those objects must be published somewhere predictable and consistent.
tldr.mechanism: Each CA has a publication point (a directory) holding its issued certificates, its CRL, a manifest and the signed objects it validates, with file extensions .cer, .crl, .mft and .roa and a recommended local cache that is synchronized top-down.
tldr.outcome: Relying parties can walk the hierarchy from their trust anchors and keep a local copy, but repositories can be briefly inconsistent, so the RFC tells them to compare against manifests and retry.

facts.label: Encoding
facts.value: DER, one object per .cer or .crl file

today: RFC 6481 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the repository structure the RPKI documents of the same period refer to, including RFC 6486 and RFC 6487.

sections.title: Why a Repository Is Needed
sections.content:
To validate attestations made in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI, see RFC 6480), relying parties (RPs) need access to all the X.509 resource certificates, certificate revocation lists (CRLs) and signed objects that make up the RPKI. Each issuer publishes its objects in an RPKI repository, and the repository system as a whole MUST be globally accessible to all RPs.

This profile defines a recommended file naming scheme, the recommended contents of each publication point (directory) and a suggested internal structure for a local repository cache. The cache is meant to ease synchronization across many publication points and to ease certification path construction.

The RFC uses three terms: a repository object is a terminal object, usually a file; a repository publication point is a collection of objects at a common place, usually a directory identified by a URI; and a repository instance is one or more publication points that share a common URI prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who signs RPKI papers needs a public place to put them, so that anyone checking those papers can fetch them. This memo says how that shared filing cabinet is organized.

sections.title: Publication Points and the Certificate Links
sections.content:
The RPKI does not require one repository instance to hold every object. The system is made of many repository instances, each made of one or more publication points. For every Certification Authority (CA) certificate there is a publication point that is authoritative for all current certificates and CRLs issued by that CA.

Two certificate extensions tie the structure together. The Subject Information Access (SIA) extension of a CA certificate holds a URI pointing to that CA's publication point. The Authority Information Access (AIA) extension of a certificate points to the authoritative location of the CA certificate under which it was issued. In the RFC's example, if certificate A has issued certificates B and C, then the AIA of B and C point to A, and the SIA of A points to a directory holding B, C and the CRL issued by A. The CRL Distribution Points extension in B and C points to that CRL.

A CA's publication point also holds all published signed objects verified by an end-entity (EE) certificate issued by that CA.

Every publication point MUST contain a manifest (RFC 6486), which lists the names and content hashes of all objects currently published by a CA or EE. An authority MAY make several changes before issuing one manifest covering them, and operators SHOULD use some directory management regime so that RPs do not see intermediate states.
sections.plainLanguage: Each certificate has two pointers: one up to the certificate that created it, and one down to the folder of things it created. Every folder also has a checklist of what should be inside.

sections.title: Object Names and What Each Publication Point Holds
sections.content:
A CA certificate has two accessMethod elements in its SIA. The id-ad-caRepository element points to the publication point of the certificates the CA issues, and the id-ad-rpkiManifest element points to the manifest object itself. A CA's publication point contains its current (non-expired, non-revoked) certificates, its most recent CRL, the current manifest and all other current signed objects verifiable with an EE certificate it issued.

  • CRL: a new CRL replaces the previous one, and CAs MUST NOT keep publishing old CRLs. The extension .crl MUST be used, and each file holds exactly one DER-encoded CRL. A non-normative naming idea is a value derived from the CA's public key: the 160-bit hash converted to a 27-character string with a modified Base64 encoding.
  • Manifest: a new manifest MUST replace the old one. The extension .mft MUST be used.
  • Certificates: a series of certificates with the same subject name, key and resources SHOULD share one filename, so each new one overwrites the last. The extension .cer MUST be used, with one DER-encoded certificate per file.
  • Signed objects: published in the publication point of the CA that issued the validating EE certificate. They MUST NOT use .crl, .mft or .cer. A Route Origination Authorization (ROA, RFC 6482) MUST use .roa.
sections.plainLanguage: The file ending tells you what a paper is, like .cer for a certificate. Newer papers of the same kind replace the old ones so the folder never holds stale copies.

sections.title: Running a Repository
sections.content:
Each issuer MAY publish its certificates and CRL in any repository. The repository SHOULD be hosted on a highly available, high-capacity platform, and it MUST be available using rsync (RFC 5781). Other retrieval mechanisms are up to the operator, but they MUST be consistent with the accessMethod values in the SIA of the related certificate.

A publication point SHOULD hold the products of its CA, and aside from subdirectories nothing else SHOULD be placed there. Any subdirectory SHOULD be the publication point of a CA or EE certificate contained in the CA directory. Signed objects live where the SIA of their EE certificate says, and that SIA points at the object rather than at a directory.

The RFC admits that a repository cannot always be consistent with its manifest. A common technique is to batch changes into a working copy of the directory and then repoint a symbolic link at it, purging the old contents later. This is non-normative and probably does not remove every chance for RPs to see an inconsistent state, so RPs SHOULD NOT assume that the repository and manifest are consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators should keep the folders on a reliable server and swap in a whole new folder at once instead of editing it in place. Even then, someone peeking at the wrong moment may see a half-done job.

sections.title: Reissuance and Key Rollover
sections.content:
If a CA certificate is reissued, for example because its set of resources changed, there should be no need to reissue everything beneath it. Because subordinate certificates carry an AIA pointing to the CA certificate's publication point, a CA SHOULD use a publication point name that persists across reissuance. A reissued CA certificate with the same subject and subject public key SHOULD overwrite the earlier one in the same place.

The same applies to key rollover (RFC 6489). The RPKI design ties a CA to a single key pair, so rollover creates a new CA certificate with a new subject name and a new key pair. The entity SHOULD keep using the same publication point for both CA instances, so AIA values further down the hierarchy stay valid. During rollover that publication point temporarily holds the CRLs and manifests of both instances, and the new CA's products overwrite those of the old CA.
sections.plainLanguage: If a school gets a new stamp, it keeps the same folder so nobody has to relabel every paper inside. For a while the folder holds papers stamped both ways, then the old ones are replaced.

sections.title: Synchronizing a Local Cache
sections.content:
An RP could build certification paths by fetching individual certificates and CRLs on demand using the AIA, SIA and CRLDP fields, but this is NOT recommended when speed and efficiency matter. Instead, each RP is recommended to keep a local repository holding a synchronized copy of all valid certificates, current CRLs and related signed objects.

The general approach is a top-down walk. It starts from locally chosen trust anchors (RFC 6490), loads their self-signed certificates as the seed, and then collects all valid certificates issued by them, applying the same steps recursively. The traversal SHOULD support a locally configured maximal chain length, so that an SIA pointer loop or another degenerate hierarchy cannot make the RP malfunction.

RPs SHOULD use the retrieved manifests to confirm they are synchronizing a current, consistent state of each publication point. Because transient inconsistency is possible, they SHOULD use a retrieval algorithm that accounts for it, for example by synchronizing twice in succession, or by fetching the manifest before and after the directory and repeating if the two copies differ.
sections.plainLanguage: To copy everything, start at the top folder you trust and open each folder inside it in turn. Stop after a set depth so a loop of folders cannot trap you, and check the checklist before and after copying.

sections.title: What the Repository Does Not Protect
sections.content:
Repositories are not assumed to be integrity-protected databases, and retrieval might be exposed to man-in-the-middle attacks. Corruption of an object is detectable because RPs validate each object's signature. Replacing a newer object with an older one is detectable through manifests, and insertion of revoked or deleted certificates is detected by processing CRLs at scheduled intervals.

Even so, manifests and CRLs cannot expose every substitution attack that uses older but still valid objects. The repository and the signed objects in it provide no confidentiality, so data under controlled access should not be put in signed objects unless some specified mechanism protects it.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can read the folders, and a sneaky person might swap in an old paper. Signatures and checklists catch most tricks but not all, and secrets do not belong there.

sections.title: Media Types and the Name Scheme Registry
sections.content:
IANA registered two media types, application/rpki-manifest (file extension .mft) and application/rpki-roa (file extension .roa). The .cer and .crl extensions come from the existing application/pkix-cert and application/pkix-crl registrations in RFC 2585.

IANA also created the RPKI Repository Name Scheme registry of three-letter filename extensions for repository objects, managed by IETF Review. It starts with the four entries .cer, .crl, .mft and .roa.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list records which file ending means which kind of paper, so everyone labels them the same way.

items.label: Certificate Revocation List
items.desc: One DER-encoded CRL per file; only the latest is kept.

items.label: Manifest
items.desc: Lists names and hashes of the objects at the publication point.

items.label: Route Origination Authorization
